mainTopic: Torah oaths versus rabbinic oaths, enforcing a rabbinic oath, a lender's oath on a שטר, and repaying a loan made in front of witnesses
overview: The גמרא finishes the second version of רב נחמן's rabbinic oath (שבועת היסת): it applies only when there is some money connection (דררא דממונא) between the two sides. Then it asks what practical difference there is between a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath. The answers keep shifting to fit different opinions. First comes turning the oath over to the claimant (מיפך שבועה). Next, the court seizing the defendant's property. Finally, moving the oath to the claimant when the defendant is חשוד על השבועה, which is done only for a Torah oath, because we do not make one enactment on top of another. According to the רבנן who don't seize property for a rabbinic obligation, a person who refuses the oath is put in שמתא for a limited time, then given lashes and left alone. Next, רב פפא rules that a borrower who claims a שטר was paid must pay, but he can demand that the lender swear. רב אשי explains how this differs from פוגם את שטרו, and רב יימר rules that the court simply does not take up the case of a צורבא מרבנן lender. Finally, רב אסי teaches that a loan made in front of witnesses must be repaid in front of witnesses. שמואל weakens this, and the גמרא begins challenging it from the משנה.

steps.title: The second version limits the oath to cases with a money connection
steps.stepSummary: Whoever attaches רב נחמן's rabbinic oath to the latter clause holds that it applies only where there is a money connection between the parties. It does not apply where the defendant denies any connection at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the one who teaches it on the latter clause says: it is only here, where there is some money connection, that the oath applies. But there, where there is no money connection, there is no oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its explanation of the second version of where רב נחמן's oath (שבועת היסת) applies. In this version, the oath is required only when the defendant admits there is some money relationship between them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the oath applies even to a total denial, so it certainly applies to the latter clause. The second version is narrower. It requires a real money link (דררא דממונא) before the rabbis impose an oath. Without such a link, a flat denial gets no oath at all.

keyTerms.meaning: teaches; here, attaches a statement to a certain part of the משנה
the latter clause of a משנה
a money connection; some admitted financial link between the parties

steps.whatToRemember: Version two: רב נחמן's oath applies only when there is a דררא דממונא, some money link between the parties. A total denial gets no oath.

phrases.english: And the one who teaches it on the latter clause –
phrases.notes: "It" is רב נחמן's rule that the defendant must take a rabbinic oath.

phrases.english: it is here that there is
a money connection [so he swears],
but there, where there is no
phrases.notes: "There" means the first clause, where the defendant says the claim has no basis at all.

phrases.english: money connection – no [oath].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the second version of רב נחמן's statement, which follows the first version given just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Under the second version, שבועת היסת applies only where there is a דררא דממונא between the parties.

steps.title: What practical difference is there between a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath differ in actual practice.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference is there between a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new practical question, and the next step will answer it. Both oaths make the defendant swear, so how do they differ in real life?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that רב נחמן has added a rabbinic oath (שבועת היסת), the גמרא wants to know whether it works just like a Torah oath. The question looks for a concrete case where the two give different outcomes.

keyTerms.meaning: an oath required by Torah law
an oath required by rabbinic law

phrases.english: What difference is there between a Torah oath
and a rabbinic oath?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין שְׁבוּעָה דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא לִשְׁבוּעָה דְּרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from where the rabbinic oath applies to how it differs from a Torah oath.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical legal difference between a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath.

steps.title: First answer: only a rabbinic oath can be turned over
steps.stepSummary: The difference is מיפך שבועה, turning the oath over to the other side. A Torah oath cannot be turned over, but a rabbinic oath can.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is turning over the oath. With a Torah oath, we do not turn it over. With a rabbinic oath, we do.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the difference is whether the defendant can say to the claimant: "You swear, and then take the money."
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a Torah oath, the defendant must either swear himself or pay. He cannot hand the oath to the claimant. With a rabbinic oath, the court allows the oath to be turned over (מפכינן) to the claimant.

keyTerms.meaning: turning the oath over to the other side

phrases.english: The difference between them is turning over the oath –
phrases.notes: The defendant says to the claimant, "Instead of me swearing, you swear and collect."

phrases.english: with a Torah oath, we do not turn over the oath,
with a rabbinic oath, we do turn it over.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A rabbinic oath can be turned over to the claimant, but a Torah oath cannot.

steps.title: According to מר בר רב אשי, a Torah oath can also be turned over
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי holds that even a Torah oath can be turned over. So according to him, what is the difference?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to מר בר רב אשי, who says that even a Torah oath can be turned over, what difference is there between a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first answer. One אמורא, מר בר רב אשי, holds that a Torah oath can also be turned over. So for him, that cannot be the difference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first answer depended on Torah oaths not being turned over. Since מר בר רב אשי turns over Torah oaths too, the two kinds of oath would work the same way in that respect. The גמרא needs a different difference that works for everyone.

phrases.english: And according to מר בר רב אשי, who says
that even with a Torah oath we turn over the oath –
what difference is there between Torah and rabbinic?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי, דְּאָמַר בִּדְאוֹרָיְיתָא נָמֵי מַפְּכִינַן שְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 3 using the opinion of מר בר רב אשי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the difference is מיפך שבועה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: מר בר רב אשי turns over Torah oaths too, so turning over cannot be the difference according to him.

steps.title: Second answer: only for a Torah oath does the court collect from property
steps.stepSummary: The difference is whether the court takes payment from the defendant's property when he will not swear. It does for a Torah oath, but not for a rabbinic oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is going down to his property. With a Torah oath, we go down to his property. With a rabbinic oath, we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new difference that works even for מר בר רב אשי. It is about whether the court can seize the defendant's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a defendant refuses a Torah oath, the court treats him as owing and collects from his property (נחתינן לנכסיה). If he refuses a rabbinic oath, the court does not collect from his property. This difference does not depend on turning over the oath, so it stands even for מר בר רב אשי.

keyTerms.meaning: going down to his property; seizing it to collect payment

steps.whatToRemember: Two differences between a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath: (1) מיפך שבועה, which is turned over only for a rabbinic oath, except according to מר בר רב אשי; (2) מיחת לנכסיה, where the court seizes property only for a Torah oath.

phrases.english: The difference between them is going down to his property –
phrases.notes: This means the court takes payment from the defendant's things when he won't swear.

phrases.english: with a Torah oath, we go down to his property,
with a rabbinic oath, we do not go down to his property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4 with a new difference.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without turning over the oath as a difference, there seemed to be no difference according to מר בר רב אשי.
steps.terutzMaskana: The difference is seizing property: done for a Torah oath, not for a rabbinic oath.

steps.title: According to רבי יוסי, the court collects from property even for rabbinic obligations
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי holds that the court seizes property even for rabbinic obligations. So according to him, what is the difference?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי יוסי, who says that even for rabbinic matters we go down to his property, what is the difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the second answer as well. The next step brings the source for רבי יוסי's view, and step 8 answers the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second answer said courts do not seize property for rabbinic obligations. But רבי יוסי holds that they do, even for rabbinic obligations. So according to him, seizing property cannot be the difference either.
steps.confusionAlert: This step ends with a question. Step 7 shows where רבי יוסי's view comes from, and step 8 gives the answer.

phrases.english: And according to רבי יוסי, who says
that even for rabbinic matters we go down to his property – [what is the difference]?
phrases.notes: The words "what is the difference" aren't written here, but the גמרא means them, just like in the last question.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, דְּאָמַר בִּדְרַבָּנַן נָמֵי נָחֲתִינַן לְנִכְסֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 5 using the opinion of רבי יוסי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the difference is מיחת לנכסיה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוסי seizes property for rabbinic obligations too, so seizing property cannot be the difference according to him.

steps.title: The source for רבי יוסי: even a rabbinic debt is collected by the court
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about found items picked up by a חרש, שוטה or קטן. Taking such an item is גזל only מפני דרכי שלום, but רבי יוסי calls it גזל גמור. רב חסדא explains that רבי יוסי still means rabbinic גזל, yet the court will take the item back. So the question returns: what difference is left between a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath?
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: When a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor finds something, taking it from them counts as robbery because of the ways of peace. רבי יוסי says: it is full robbery. And רב חסדא said: full robbery by rabbinic law. What is the practical difference? That the judges take it back from the taker. So what difference is there between a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is proving the claim it made in step 6, that רבי יוסי lets the court seize property even for a rabbinic obligation. It then repeats the question that this raises.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By Torah law a חרש, שוטה or קטן cannot acquire a found item, so taking it from them is only rabbinic robbery. Even so, according to רב חסדא, רבי יוסי holds that the court will actually take it back by force. That cancels the difference from step 5, so a new difference between Torah and rabbinic oaths is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: A deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, and a minor. They lack legal ability to acquire by Torah law.
Because of the ways of peace. This is a rabbinic rule made to prevent fighting.
From their words, meaning by rabbinic law
To have it taken back by the judges

phrases.english: As we learned: a found item of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor,

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ בָּהֶם גָּזֵל מִפְּנֵי דַּרְכֵי שָׁלוֹם.
phrases.english: taking it counts as robbery because of the ways of peace.
Rabbi Yosei says: it is full robbery.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: גָּזֵל גָּמוּר – מִדִּבְרֵיהֶם.
phrases.english: And Rav Chisda said: full robbery, by their (the Rabbis') words.
phrases.notes: So even רבי יוסי agrees it is only rabbinic robbery, not Torah robbery.

phrases.english: What is the practical difference?
To have it taken out by the judges.
So what is the difference between a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the claim about רבי יוסי in step 6 and restates the challenge.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יוסי lets the court seize property for a rabbinic obligation
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in גיטין about found items of a חרש, שוטה וקטן, as explained by רב חסדא
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 5, that only Torah oaths lead the court to seize property
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוסי has the court collect even rabbinic debts, so seizing property no longer separates the two kinds of oath.

steps.title: The difference is when the defendant is suspected of swearing falsely
steps.stepSummary: Suppose the defendant is חשוד על השבועה. For a Torah oath, the court moves the oath over to the claimant. For a rabbinic oath it does not, because moving the oath is itself a rabbinic rule, and we do not make one rabbinic rule on top of another.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is when the defendant is suspected about oaths. For a Torah oath, if the defendant is suspected, we turn the oath over and put it on the other side. For a rabbinic oath, the oath itself is a rabbinic enactment, and we do not make an enactment on top of an enactment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new difference between a Torah oath and a rabbinic oath that works even for רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the defendant cannot be trusted to swear, the רבנן arranged for the claimant to swear and collect. This arrangement applies to a Torah oath. A rabbinic oath like היסת is already a rabbinic enactment, so a second enactment is not added on top of it.

keyTerms.meaning: The one opposite him, meaning the defendant facing the claimant
Suspected of swearing falsely, so not trusted to take an oath
We turn over, meaning we move the oath to the other person
We do not make one rabbinic enactment on top of another

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the same as מיפך שבועה from step 3. There, the defendant chooses to hand the oath to the claimant. Here, the court moves the oath because the defendant cannot be trusted.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them
where the one opposite him is suspected about oaths;
with a Torah oath, if the one opposite him is suspected about oaths,
we turn the oath over onto the other one;
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the word in round brackets.

phrases.english: with a rabbinic oath, it is an enactment,
and we do not make an enactment on top of an enactment.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ שֶׁכְּנֶגְדּוֹ חָשׁוּד עַל הַשְּׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רבי יוסי's view.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Once רבי יוסי seizes property even for rabbinic debts, there seemed to be no difference left.
steps.terutzMaskana: A difference remains: only a Torah oath is moved to the claimant when the defendant is חשוד.

steps.title: What do the רבנן do to someone who refuses a rabbinic oath?
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן who disagree with רבי יוסי say the court does not seize property for a rabbinic obligation. So how do they deal with a person who refuses to take a rabbinic oath?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the רבנן who disagree with רבי יוסי, who say that for a rabbinic matter we do not go down into his property, what do we do to him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical follow-up question about how the court enforces a rabbinic oath according to the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said the court does not take property from someone who refuses a rabbinic oath. Without some kind of pressure, a rabbinic oath would have no force. The גמרא wants to know what pressure the court actually uses.

keyTerms.meaning: We go down into his property, meaning we seize his assets
What do we do to him?

phrases.english: And according to the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Yosei,
who say that in a rabbinic matter
we do not go down into his property,
what do we do to him?
phrases.notes: He means the person who refuses to take the rabbinic oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the רבנן's view from step 5 and asks how they enforce a rabbinic oath.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What sanction the court uses on a person who refuses a rabbinic oath, if it does not seize his property

steps.title: We place him in שמתא
steps.stepSummary: The court puts him in שמתא, a ban, until he agrees to swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: We place him under a ban.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the court puts the refuser in שמתא instead of taking his money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court does not take his property. Instead it pressures him socially and religiously with a ban, so that he will agree to swear.

keyTerms.meaning: We place him in a ban
A ban. The person is kept apart from the community.

phrases.english: We place him under a ban.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The court uses שמתא as the sanction.

steps.title: רבינא: a ban is no gentler than taking his money
steps.stepSummary: רבינא tells רב אשי that a ban is like squeezing a man so hard that he will give up his cloak just to get free. That is no lighter than seizing his property. So what do we really do to him?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: This is grabbing him by his private parts so that he will let go of his cloak! Rather, what do we do to him?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges the answer of שמתא and asks again what the court does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole idea of the רבנן was to be gentler with rabbinic obligations and not seize property. But a ban pressures him so much that he will pay anyway, so in practice it is no different from seizing his property. That seems to defeat the purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: Grabbing him by his private parts. This is an image of extreme pressure.
Rather. It introduces a demand for a different answer.

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
This is grabbing him by his private parts
so that he lets go of his cloak!
Rather, what do we do to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of שמתא in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that we place him in שמתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ban pressures him into paying anyway, so it is no gentler than seizing his property. The רבנן specifically refused to seize property.

steps.title: רב אשי: a limited ban, then lashes, then we leave him alone
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that the ban is not open-ended. It lasts only until the time for lashes. Then he is given lashes and left alone, without the court ever forcing payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We ban him until the time comes to give him lashes, and then we give him lashes and leave him alone.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי limits the sanction so that it does not turn into forced payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban has a fixed end point. After that he receives lashes, and the matter is closed. The court never takes his money, so the רבנן's rule that we do not seize property for a rabbinic obligation stays in place.
steps.whatToRemember: According to the רבנן, a person who refuses a rabbinic oath is put under a ban for a limited time, then given lashes and left alone. The court does not seize his property.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מְשַׁמְּתִינַן לֵיהּ עַד דְּמָטֵי זְמַן נִגְדֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: We ban him until the time for his lashes arrives,
phrases.notes: He means the point when a stubborn person under a ban may be given lashes.

phrases.english: and we give him lashes and leave him alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מְשַׁמְּתִינַן לֵיהּ עַד דְּמָטֵי זְמַן נִגְדֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge by limiting how long the ban lasts.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ban would continue until he gave in and paid, which works like seizing his property.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban lasts only until the time for lashes. Then he gets lashes and is left alone, and no payment is forced.

steps.title: A borrower who claims the note was already paid
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that a borrower who says the שטר was paid must pay anyway. But if he asks for it, the lender must swear that he was not paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Someone brings a loan document against his friend, and the friend says, 'That document was already paid.' We tell the borrower, 'You can't just say that. Go pay.' But if the borrower says, 'Let him swear to me,' we tell the lender, 'Swear to him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ruling from רב פפא about a borrower who says a loan document was already paid off.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A valid שטר is strong proof, so the borrower's bare word that he paid does not cancel it. Still, he can make the lender take an oath that the debt is really unpaid before the lender collects.

keyTerms.meaning: A written loan document, a promissory note
It is not in your power; your word alone is not enough

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule that the rest of the section questions and refines.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי מַאן דְּאַפֵּיק שְׁטָרָא עַל חַבְרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: One who brings out a loan document against his fellow,
and the other says to him: The document is paid,
we say to him: It is not in your power,
phrases.notes: Here 'him' is the borrower. His word alone can't cancel a valid document.

phrases.english: go pay.
But if he says: Let him swear to me,
phrases.notes: The borrower wants the lender to swear that he really was not paid.

phrases.english: we say to him: Swear to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: הַאי מַאן דְּאַפֵּיק שְׁטָרָא עַל חַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of rabbinic oaths and שמתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A borrower who claims a שטר was paid must pay. If he demands it, the lender swears first.

steps.title: How is this different from a lender who admits partial payment?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרבא asks רב אשי how רב פפא's case differs from פוגם את שטרו, where the lender also has to swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא, the son of רבא, said to רב אשי: So what is the difference between this case and a lender who weakens his own document?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בריה דרבא challenges רב פפא by comparing his case to the known case of פוגם את שטרו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a lender admits he got part of the money (פוגם את שטרו), the חכמים made him swear before he collects the rest. If, as רב פפא says, every lender with a שטר can be made to swear, the special oath of פוגם seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: A lender who weakens his own document by admitting he was partly paid
What is the difference between this and

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha the son of Rava said to Rav Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה בֵּין זֶה לְפוֹגֵם אֶת שְׁטָרוֹ?
phrases.english: And what is the difference between this and one who weakens his document?
phrases.notes: This is the case where the lender admits he got part of the money. He must swear before collecting the rest.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָה בֵּין זֶה לְפוֹגֵם אֶת שְׁטָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's rule from step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's ruling that any lender with a שטר can be made to swear
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If every lender swears when asked, the special rule that a פוגם את שטרו swears seems to make no difference.

steps.title: In one case the court raises the claim; in the other the borrower must
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that in פוגם, the court demands the oath on its own. In רב פפא's case, the lender swears only if the borrower asks.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, even if the borrower doesn't make the claim himself, we make it for him. Here, we tell him, 'Go pay him.' Only if he makes the claim and says, 'Swear to me,' do we tell the lender, 'Go swear to him.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives the difference between the two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פוגם case, the court itself raises the claim for the borrower, so the lender always swears. In a plain case, the court tells the borrower to pay. An oath happens only if the borrower himself asks for one.

keyTerms.meaning: We, the court, make the claim for him

steps.confusionAlert: Both lenders may end up swearing. The difference is who starts it: in פוגם, the court does; in the plain case, only the borrower can.

phrases.english: He said to him: There,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא טָעֵין אִיהוּ –
phrases.english: even though he himself does not claim,
we claim for him;

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא, אָמְרִינַן לֵיהּ: זִיל שַׁלֵּים לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: here, we say to him: Go pay him,
and if he claims and says: Swear to me,
we say to him: Go swear to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם, אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא טָעֵין אִיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two cases seem the same, since the lender swears in both.
steps.terutzMaskana: In פוגם, the court raises the oath on its own. In a plain case, an oath happens only when the borrower demands it.

steps.title: A Torah scholar lender is not made to swear
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי adds that if the lender is a צורבא מרבנן, the court does not make him swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the lender is a Torah scholar, we do not make him swear.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי adds an exception to the rule he just explained.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a borrower can demand that the lender swear. According to this addition, a lender who is a צורבא מרבנן is not put under oath. The next step questions what this would mean for the borrower.

phrases.english: And if he is a Torah scholar,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the lender, the one holding the document.

phrases.english: we do not make him swear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב אשי's words, adding an exception for a scholar.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lender who is a צורבא מרבנן is not made to swear.

steps.title: Can a scholar just take people's money?
steps.stepSummary: רב יימר objects: if the scholar does not swear, he would collect with no check at all, as if a scholar could take people's money.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יימר said to רב אשי: Can a Torah scholar strip people of their cloaks?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יימר challenges the exception for a צורבא מרבנן that רב אשי just gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the scholar is excused from the oath and still collects, the borrower loses the protection the oath was meant to give. Being a scholar does not give a person the right to take money that may not be his.

keyTerms.meaning: Stripping off a cloak; a picture for taking someone's money

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יֵימַר לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Yeimar said to Rav Ashi:
Can a Torah scholar strip off people's cloaks?!
phrases.notes: He means: can a scholar collect money with no oath, when the borrower says he already paid?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the scholar exception in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a צורבא מרבנן lender is not made to swear
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Excusing him from the oath would let him collect from a borrower who may have already paid, which is unfair.

steps.title: The court does not take up the scholar's case
steps.stepSummary: רב יימר corrects the rule: the court does not make the scholar swear, but it also does not get involved in his case to collect for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, we do not take up his case at all.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יימר gives the corrected version of the rule for a צורבא מרבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court does not force an oath on the scholar out of respect. But it also will not help him collect. He keeps his dignity, and the borrower keeps his money.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; it must be this way instead
We get involved with, we take up

steps.whatToRemember: A borrower who claims he paid a valid שטר must pay, but he can demand that the lender swear. In פוגם את שטרו, the court requires the oath even without being asked. If the lender is a צורבא מרבנן, the court neither makes him swear nor helps him collect.

phrases.english: Rather, we do not attend to his case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge in step 17 by changing the scholar exception.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A צורבא מרבנן lender is not made to swear, but the court does not take up his case, so he cannot collect through it.

steps.title: A loan made with witnesses must be repaid with witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a new line of the משנה, then brings רב אסי's rule: if you lend in front of witnesses, the borrower must repay in front of witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: "I have a מנה in your hand," and so on. רב יהודה said in the name of רב אסי: someone who lends money to his friend in front of witnesses, the borrower must repay him in front of witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting the opening words of the next משנה case. Then it brings רב אסי's rule about repaying a loan that was made in front of witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אסי holds that a loan made in front of witnesses can only be cleared by a repayment made in front of witnesses. So if the borrower just says "I paid you" with no witnesses, he is not believed and still owes the money.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of one hundred דינרים

phrases.english: "I have a maneh in your hand," etc.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב אַסִּי:
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav Asi said:
One who lends to his friend in front of witnesses,
must be repaid in front of witnesses.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic on a new line of the משנה. It is unrelated to the צורבא מרבנן discussion that came before.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A loan made in front of witnesses must be repaid in front of witnesses. Otherwise the borrower's claim that he paid is not accepted.

steps.title: שמואל: the borrower can say his witnesses went overseas
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה reports that שמואל disagreed. The borrower can say he paid in front of two people who have since left the country.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: when I said this rule in front of שמואל, he told me that the borrower can say to the lender, "I paid you in front of so-and-so and so-and-so, and they went overseas."
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה tells us that when he repeated רב אסי's rule to שמואל, שמואל did not accept it as stated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל points out a gap in רב אסי's rule. The borrower can claim he did pay in front of witnesses, just witnesses who are no longer around. That makes the demand for repayment witnesses practically empty, since the borrower can always claim this.

phrases.english: When I said it in front of Shmuel,
phrases.notes: The "I" here is רב יהודה, still speaking.

phrases.english: he said to me: he can say to him:
"I repaid you in front of so-and-so and so-and-so,
and they went off overseas."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: שמואל reacts to רב אסי's rule and weakens it in practice.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the practical force of רב אסי's rule that repayment requires witnesses.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The borrower can always claim he paid in front of witnesses who are now overseas, so demanding witnesses does not really protect the lender.

steps.title: Challenge to רב אסי from the משנה's case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: the borrower admits the debt, then the next day says "I paid you," and he is פטור. Admitting in front of witnesses is like borrowing in front of witnesses, yet he is believed without repayment witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: "I have a מנה in your hand." He answered, "Yes." The next day he said, "Give it to me." He answered, "I gave it to you." He is פטור. But here, since the claim was made in front of witnesses, it is like he lent him the money in front of witnesses, and still the משנה teaches that he is פטור!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אסי using the משנה. In the משנה, a borrower who admitted a debt in front of witnesses is believed when he later says he paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The admission in front of witnesses works like a loan made in front of witnesses. By רב אסי's rule, the borrower should need witnesses to prove he repaid. Yet the משנה says he is פטור just on his word, so this looks like a contradiction to רב אסי.

phrases.english: We learned: "I have a maneh in your hand,"
he said to him, "Yes";
the next day he said to him: "Give it to me,"
"I gave it to you": he is exempt.
But here, since he claimed it from him in front of witnesses,
it is like one who lent him in front of witnesses,
and yet it teaches that he is exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רב אסי's rule from step 19 and attacks it from the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אסי's rule that a loan made with witnesses must be repaid with witnesses.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An admission in front of witnesses is like a loan in front of witnesses. Yet the משנה believes the borrower's claim that he paid without any repayment witnesses, which goes against רב אסי.
steps.confusionAlert: The משנה never says "witnesses" outright. The whole question rests on the גמרא's assumption that the admission happened in front of witnesses, which makes it like a loan made in front of witnesses.
